c.name: Rulers' demand for a human audience, service and company (status, vicarious leisure, sex)
c.mechanism: MERGED from 'Audience and status demand' and 'Demand for human service, company and sex'. (a) Status is relational and needs others to grant it. Autocrats spend heavily on cults of personality, mass spectacles and benefactions that buy admiration rather than labor or taxes: Paul Veyne, Bread and Circuses (1976; English 1990), on Roman euergetism as giving for honor (exact argument not verified this session); Lisa Wedeen, Ambiguities of Domination (1999), on the Assad cult; Jan Plamper, The Stalin Cult (2012). Wikipedia 'Cult of personality' (fetched) cites mainly legitimation and consolidation explanations, so the published mechanism is mostly instrumental; the 'admiration for its own sake' reading is weaker and largely inference. (b) Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899): servants and retainers are kept to display the master's wealth ('vicarious leisure'), not for output; human service is a luxury good valued because humans do it. Example: North Korea's Kippumjo, about 2,000 women and girls kept to entertain senior officials, including sexually (Wikipedia, citing Bradley K. Martin, Under the Loving Care of the Fatherly Leader, 2004). Ottoman and Mughal harems and royal households ran from hundreds to a few thousand people.
cases: None found that meets rule 2: no case where a ruler with capacity for mass killing held back and the restraint is attributed to wanting admiration, an audience, or human service.

Supporting but not qualifying: North Korean mass games and the Stalin cult show demand for displayed adoration (Plamper 2012), but both regimes killed or imprisoned huge numbers, so the demand coexisted with mass repression.
Kippumjo and royal harems show demand for human service at the scale of thousands, coexisting with mass repression (North Korean political prison camps, UN Commission of Inquiry 2014).
c.parameterization: Either (a) a per-bloc value on the surviving population, U_status = s_aud * g(N_alive/N0) with g concave or saturating, added to every option and shrinking with deaths each option causes, with a wide prior; or (b) a floor N_serve (coalition size x retinue size x dependants) acting as a minimum on rem or a penalty on options that take the population below it.
c.overlap: Strong overlap with rem (captive remnant of 0.03 to 0.1%, about 2.4 to 8 million). The documented demand (thousands to perhaps millions across all elites) sits at or below the remnant. Partial overlap with alpha_med: the motive is self-regarding rather than other-regarding, but it enters the utility the same way. AI-generated audiences or co-opted elites could substitute. Distinct only if g saturates far above the remnant size, and nothing in the evidence shows that. Survivors held as servants would still count as disempowered, so it does not change the outcome category.
c.survives_A3_A6: The motive survives (psychological, not leverage). But it restrains little: its marginal value is likely saturated by the remnant (which A11 allows), a co-opted elite or synthetic admirers. Evidence that peers are the audience that matters points the same way. Likely fails rules 2 and 3.

Stalin's cult (Plamper 2012), North Korea's mass games and the Kippumjo all sit next to purges and political prison camps (UN Commission of Inquiry on the DPRK, 2014). Rule 1 is only partly met. Veblen (1899) documents demand for human service as conspicuous display. The cult-of-personality literature (Wedeen 1999, Plamper 2012) mostly gives instrumental explanations: legitimation and consolidation. None of it gives a published causal account of status demand restraining rulers from killing. The "admiration for its own sake" brake is inference, as the candidate admits. Rule 3 is doubtful too. The documented scale of the demand (thousands, at most millions) fits inside the existing captive remnant parameter rem (about 2.4 to 8 million), so the brake would mostly duplicate rem and alpha_med. I could not run new searches: the session's web search limit (200) was used up. I did not personally re-check the cited sources, but the refutation rests on the candidate's own admitted lack of qualifying cases, so it does not depend on that check.

c.name: Rulers' self-risk from the means of killing (loss of control of AI/autonomous force, and method blowback)
c.mechanism: MERGED from 'Fear of one's own instrument' and 'Blowback from the means of killing'. (a) Coup-proofing: autocrats weaken, split or stack their own coercive forces because those forces are the main threat to them (Quinlivan, 'Coup-Proofing: Its Practice and Consequences in the Middle East', International Security 24(2), 1999; Talmadge, The Dictator's Army, 2015). Carried to closure: a ruler may hold back from fielding fully autonomous mass-killing capacity, or from giving it open-ended targeting, for fear that it, a rival who controls it, or a misaligned AI turns on him. (b) Self-spreading or planet-wide methods (biological agents, large nuclear use, ecosystem poisoning) can come back on perpetrators' forces, food supply and shelters. Nuclear-winter research (Xia et al. 2022, Nature Food, as summarized in Wikipedia 'Nuclear winter') projects famine deaths in the billions after a large exchange, reaching bunkered elites through food. Counter-evidence: PAHO/WHO guidance says unburied bodies after mass deaths pose little epidemic risk (Morgan 2004, Rev Panam Salud Publica; not fetched, needs checking), so killing as such may carry little blowback; only certain methods do.
cases: Coup-proofing (Saddam's parallel guard units, Gulf monarchies; Quinlivan 1999) shows rulers limiting their own forces out of fear, but the restraint was on military effectiveness, not on repression; parallel forces were often used for repression.

Zhejiang-Jiangxi campaign 1942: Unit 731 left paratyphoid and anthrax in food and wells; Japanese troops entering contaminated areas suffered 'upward from 10,000' casualties per a 1944 POW, and official records show more than 1,700 cholera deaths (Wikipedia 'Zhejiang-Jiangxi campaign'; Tanaka, Hidden Horrors, 1996; Scott, Target Tokyo, 2015). No documented claim it restrained later Japanese biological use.

US 1969: Nixon ended the offensive biological weapons program on 25 Nov 1969, calling the weapons 'unreliable'; National Security Archive (NSAEBB58) records scientists' advice on 'high risk and limited utility'. Reachable documents do not attribute the decision to fear of losing control or blowback on the US population; political criticism, doubts about military usefulness and fear of a 'poor man's atom bomb' dominate. Tucker and Mahan NDU case study (2009) could not be opened (HTTP 403). It restrained a weapon in interstate war, not killing of a population.
c.parameterization: A ruler-perceived cost on depopulate and on h_use: c_ctl * P_loss(AI capability) for loss of control (or a ruler-perceived AI-takeover hazard triggered by deploying the means, lowering h_use or delaying effective dL_means), plus a method-specific self-cost c_blow scaling with how uncontrollable the method is, shifting execution toward slower methods (longer T_full, more strangulation/neglect deaths). For nuclear collusion, lower s_bunk by a nuclear-winter famine factor.
c.overlap: The model has AI takeover as a background end point and mc_ai, but no control-loss cost that rulers perceive when ordering deployment; partly overlaps with k_prg and c_cc for elite rivals. The wide U(0.2, 1.0) range on h_use may absorb hesitation; the abstract means (dL_means, h_use), c_self, s_bunk (A9) and nuclear deterrence cover much of the blowback part. Direction is ambiguous: fear of the instrument may push toward tight control rather than non-use, and coup-proofing historically shifted coercion rather than reducing it. Blowback mainly changes which method and how fast, not whether.
c.survives_A3_A6: Yes: the control-loss part depends on the AI itself and gets stronger as automation grows; blowback is physical and biological. But substitution weakens it: under A9, strangulation and neglect have no epidemic blowback onto bunkered elites and alone reach 99.9% within T_full. No case attributes restraint from mass killing to either strand, so it likely fails rule 2 unless a Jev elicitation is accepted on analog cases.

v.reasons:
Rule 2 fails. The protocol needs at least two historical cases where the restraint is attributed to this mechanism, and the candidate offers at most one.

(1) Coup-proofing (Quinlivan 1999, Talmadge 2015) is a documented mechanism. But by the candidate's own account it held back military effectiveness, not repression or killing. Parallel guard units were often the tools of repression. That is restraint on the instrument, not on killing, so it is not a case of rulers being stopped from mass killing.

(2) Zhejiang-Jiangxi 1942 records blowback on Japanese troops. There is no documented claim that it restrained later Japanese biological use, so it shows blowback happening, not restraint.

(3) The US in 1969 is the only usable case, and it is stronger than the candidate says. I checked Nixon's 25 Nov 1969 statement (American Presidency Project, presidency.ucsb.edu). He gives the reason in so many words: "Biological weapons have massive, unpredictable and potentially uncontrollable consequences. They may produce global epidemics and impair the health of future generations." So the public rationale names uncontrollability and blowback. But the National Security Archive material (NSAEBB58) also points to limited military use and political motives, so the cause is mixed. It also restrained a weapon of interstate war, not mass killing of a population.

That leaves one partial case where two are required, and no case at all for the loss-of-control-of-AI strand. A Jev elicitation can set strengths under the protocol, but it cannot stand in for case evidence under rule 2.

Two weaker problems:
- The direction is unclear. Fear of one's own instrument historically shifted coercion around (tighter control, parallel forces) rather than reducing it.
- The PAHO/WHO counter-evidence suggests killing as such carries little blowback; only some methods do. The candidate itself says this source (Morgan 2004) was not fetched, and I did not fetch it either.
v.rule_results: Rule 1 (documented mechanism): partial pass. Coup-proofing is documented for the fear-of-own-forces strand, but it restrains how effective the forces are, not repression. The blowback strand rests on nuclear-winter and bioweapon physical effects, with no political-science account that it restrains rulers. Rule 2 (two attributed cases): FAIL. Only the US 1969 case attributes restraint to uncontrollability (Nixon statement verified), and its motives were mixed and the setting interstate. Coup-proofing and Zhejiang-Jiangxi do not show rulers restrained from killing by this mechanism. Rule 3 (model-expressible, not already carried): plausible but partly overlaps with h_use range, c_self, s_bunk and nuclear deterrence (not the focus of this lens). A3-A6 survival: control-loss strand survives in principle; blowback strand is undercut by substitution to strangulation/neglect under A9.

v.reasons: Refuted on model fit, and rule 2 fails as well. (1) Blowback strand: the model already carries it. The fast means is a single abstract parameter (dL_means, h_use U(0.2,1)), the rulers' own-survival cost is c_self with s_bunk under A9, and nuclear deterrence is separate. Under A9, strangulation and neglect reach 99.9% within T_full with no epidemic or famine blowback onto bunkered elites. The paper's own ablation (paper.md around line 1032) bounds the whole channel: removing the means of mass killing entirely (A8 off) moves the headline from about 0.447 to 0.434. A brake that only changes the method can do no more than that, and the candidate itself says blowback "changes which method and how fast, not whether". The nuclear-winter famine factor is a re-range of s_bunk inside the existing A9 collusion rule (collude iff b_col > (1-s_bunk) x p_nx x c_self), not a new brake. (2) Control-loss strand: it partly overlaps with k_pg (narrow-group power-grab hazard at full automation), k_prg/c_cc (purges and counter-coups) and the background AI-takeover end point. Its direction is ambiguous. The coup-proofing evidence (Quinlivan 1999, Talmadge 2015) shows rulers re-shaping and splitting coercion, often keeping parallel forces for repression, not refraining from repression. So no causal sign can be justified, and at most it justifies the existing wide h_use range. (3) Rule 2: none of the three cases credits restraint from mass repression or killing to either strand. Coup-proofing limited military effectiveness, not repression. Zhejiang-Jiangxi 1942 had blowback but no record that it restrained later use. The US 1969 decision was about interstate weapons, and the sources reached do not credit it to loss of control or blowback. On A3 to A6, the mechanism would survive because it is physical and AI-based, but surviving does not save it once rules 2 and 3 fail.

c.name: Intrinsic demand for legitimacy, recognition and legacy (including concern for posterity)
c.mechanism: MERGED from 'Legacy and posterity' and 'Intrinsic demand for legitimacy, recognition and legacy'. Rulers may value being seen as rightful by subjects and by history as a good in itself. Gerschewski, 'The three pillars of stability', Democratization 20(1), 2013 (not fetched), treats legitimation as a separate pillar, though mainly instrumental. The non-instrumental part is legacy concern: a ruler who prefers losing power to being remembered for mass killing. Recognition from subjects needs living subjects, so depopulation destroys it regardless of outside enforcement. Counter-evidence: concern for historical reputation often produces concealment, not restraint. Himmler's Posen speeches (October 1943) called the extermination 'a glorious chapter that has not and will not be spoken of'; Sonderaktion 1005 from 1943 exhumed and burned bodies to destroy evidence (Wikipedia, Posen speeches). The paper itself lists 'rulers' own demand for human legitimacy or company' as a missing brake (Section 8, limitation 4).
cases: Shah of Iran 1978-79: with an intact army, he told Western contemporaries 'he would rather leave the country than fire on his own people' and left in January 1979 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Reza_Pahlavi). Confounders in the same source: cancer, indecision, Western allies judging the monarchy unsaveable. Partial restraint (an estimated 540 to 2,000 revolution deaths). Abbas Milani, The Shah (2011), discusses this (not fetched).

Gorbachev 1989 (shared with the protective-doctrine candidate): if read as reputation and international standing rather than doctrine. Levesque (1997) supports a values reading; the legacy-specific attribution is inference.

Counter-cases: Posen speeches and Aktion 1005 show reputation concern leading to secrecy and evidence destruction while killing continued. No second clean case of legacy-attributed restraint, so rule 2 probably not met.
c.parameterization: A recognition payoff g_rec x (surviving population share) x (welfare under the option) added to each member's utility, with no B3 scaling by outsiders' kinetic power; depopulation loses it all. Strength via Jev elicitation given thin cases. Alternatively a non-fading recurring illegitimacy cost (inverse of phi_stigma).
c.overlap: E0 ('legitimacy + international pressure') is scaled under B3 by outsiders' enforcement power and vanishes once a bloc dominates, so intrinsic legitimacy is not E0 after B3. Closest: phi_stigma, moral_med, alpha_med. The posterity component is largely carried by phi_stigma and E0, and in the cases legacy cannot be separated from conscience.
c.survives_A3_A6: Partly. The instrumental part (legitimacy as cheaper substitute for repression) does not survive. The intrinsic part lives in preferences and survives, but: (1) sel_top plausibly filters it at the top; (2) after closure the audience may shift to peers, rival rulers or AI systems; (3) after near-total depopulation the perpetrators and their AI write the history, so the posterity audience is controlled. Wide range if included.

It gives no reasons and no attribution to legacy or concern with being legitimate. The candidate's own source lists strong confounders: cancer, indecision, and US/Western judgement that the monarchy could not be saved. c.name: Protective doctrine held by the rulers themselves (mirror image of the depopulation ideology)
c.mechanism: A doctrine sincerely held by the ruling group (divine judgment, dharma, universalist humanism) makes mass killing costly in rulers' own terms, independent of any audience. The model has the harmful version (p_id, id_share, id_mor; Bandura 1999, moral justification) but no protective version. Jacques Levesque, The Enigma of 1989 (UC Press, 1997), argues Soviet non-use of force came from a 'new ideology of transition ... based on new, universal values', not mere weakness (verified via https://www.ucpress.edu/books/the-enigma-of-1989/paper). Archie Brown, The Gorbachev Factor (OUP, 1996), similar (not fetched).
cases: Gorbachev and Eastern Europe 1989: large Soviet forces present and precedents of 1956 and 1968, yet no intervention; Levesque (1997) attributes this to new thinking. Counter-reading: Wikipedia 'Sinatra Doctrine' stresses economic decay and Afghanistan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinatra_Doctrine). Lethal force was used in Tbilisi 1989, Baku 1990, Vilnius 1991.

Ashoka after Kalinga (c. 260 BCE): Rock Edict XIII records remorse over 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported and renunciation of conquest by dhamma while keeping the army (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalinga_War). Caveats: some scholars call the narrative propaganda, conversion was gradual, and the edict warns forest peoples his power remains (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashoka; Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas, 1961, not fetched).

Theodosius's penance 390 (weak): ruler submitted to a doctrinal sanction he believed in, but the account is disputed and came after the killing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Thessalonica).
c.parameterization: A protective-ideology process mirroring the existing one: yearly hazard p_pid that a bloc's rulers hold a protective doctrine, half-life (reuse id_hl), and when held at level pid_lev a multiplier (1 + k_pid x pid_lev) on mm, applied to all coalition members jointly and not reduced by sel_top. Strengths from cases (wide) or Jev elicitation.
c.overlap: moral_med carries individual conscience (with m_pow, sel_top, k_mor lowering it). Distinct parts: shared and correlated across the coalition; time-varying and adoptable, symmetric with p_id; not necessarily filtered by selection (Ashoka and Gorbachev reached the top first). If a wide moral_med tail is judged to cover it, it fails rule 3. Distinct in structure, modestly distinct in content.
c.survives_A3_A6: Yes in principle: works through rulers' beliefs. Weakness is evidence: Gorbachev is confounded by material constraints, Ashoka's edicts are self-presentation, and neither shows restraint of rulers facing no public at all.

v.reasons:
Under the mechanism-and-cases lens, the candidate passes, but only just. No rule clearly fails. Rule 1 is met. The UC Press description of Levesque (1997) says Soviet passivity in 1989 was "not just a sign of Soviet weakness" and points to "a new ideology of transition" built on universal values. That is a published causal account of rulers' own doctrine restraining them. Bandura's moral-justification work, which the model already uses for the harmful version, gives the general mechanism, run in reverse. Scott Straus, Making and Unmaking Nations (Cornell UP, 2015), may also support this, but I could not check it (the publisher page did not load) and it was not used.

Rule 2 is met by two cases of limited quality. (a) Gorbachev 1989: Levesque explicitly credits the non-intervention to the new ideology. But this reading is contested by material explanations, such as economic decay and Afghanistan (see the Wikipedia Sinatra Doctrine page). The doctrine also did not stop lethal force inside the USSR (Tbilisi, Baku, Vilnius), so it restrained foreign intervention more than killing at home. (b) Ashoka: Rock Edict XIII, as quoted on Wikipedia's Kalinga War page, ties remorse and the turn to dhamma to the Kalinga killings, and about 40 years of relative peace followed. However, Wikipedia's Ashoka page cites John S. Strong calling the inscriptions "propaganda", notes that conversion was gradual, and reports that Eggermont argues he converted before Kalinga. So the attribution rests mainly on the ruler's own account. (c) Theodosius fails as a restraint case: the sources are disputed, the penance came after the massacre, and the 30-day waiting law cannot be tied to it with any confidence (Wikipedia, Massacre of Thessalonica).

Net: two cases where the evidence credits the doctrine, both confounded or self-reported. Per the protocol, weak evidence calls for a wide strength range, not exclusion. The bigger risk is rule 3 (overlap with moral_med), which belongs to the other reviewer's lens.

Theodosius fails: disputed, and the penance came after the killing. Rule 3 (model-expressible and not already in the model): not assessed under this lens. A parameterization is given, but overlap with moral_med is the main risk. A3-A6 survival: plausible, since it works through rulers' beliefs and not labor or revolt, but no case shows restraint with no audience at all.

v.reasons: On model fit, the candidate passes, with one caveat. Its fixed level is already in the model. moral_med (models/m8_v4.py line 327, applied at line 900) is drawn once per run and shared by every coalition member and every bloc, so a high draw is already a doctrine-like moral cost the whole coalition holds together. Members differ only through mem_zm. The candidate's claim that the shared part is new is therefore wrong. What the model lacks is a channel that raises moral cost after it starts. In the mm chain (lines 1525 to 1530), moral cost only falls over time or by bloc: m_pow, the k_mor decay, ruthless x0.5, and id_mor removal when the p_id ideology is held. Nothing raises it. A bloc-specific adoption hazard (p_pid, decaying over id_hl, multiplier 1 + k_pid x pid_lev on mm) would be the mirror of p_id/id_lev. It could be added in the same place in the code, and no existing parameter carries it. A wider moral_med cannot copy it, because a run-level draw cannot make one bloc's rulers convert partway through the run. Only the adoption hazard should count as new. Its strength should be limited to conversion cases, not to the baseline humanism already behind moral_med (Sagan and Valentino polls). The plan to skip the sel_top reduction needs stating, since it overrides B1 selection. It is defensible only for doctrines adopted after reaching the top (Ashoka, Gorbachev), which is how the cases read. On A3 to A6, the mechanism runs through rulers' own beliefs, not labor, enforcers or revolt, so it survives. A multiplier on mm would still be worn down by the k_mor decay and mc_ai automation distance, which is consistent with the model. Whether the cases support it (Gorbachev's material constraints, Ashoka's self-presentation) is for the other reviewer.

range.name: Protective doctrine held by the rulers (p_pid, k_pid)
range.parameter: There are two new parameters plus a reused one. p_pid is the probability that a bloc's ruling group comes to sincerely hold a protective doctrine (religious, dharmic or universalist humanist) within 9 years, if no other driver acts. It mirrors p_id: it is converted to a yearly hazard, adoption is reduced to 0.1x before closure, and the doctrine fades with half-life id_hl (reused). The held level pid_lev builds over about 4 years, the same as id_lev. k_pid is the strength. While the doctrine is held, the moral-cost multiplier mm becomes mm x (1 + k_pid x pid_lev), the same for every member of that bloc's coalition. It therefore raises mXk and mXn, the moral cost of killing and of neglect, in the elite game. A flag pid_on switches it on and is off in the baseline, so the brake can be reported alone and together with the others, as the protocol requires. Only adoption after the run starts, specific to one bloc, counts as new (verifier 2). The run-level shared level is already carried by moral_med.
range.distribution: p_pid ~ lognormal, median 0.065, sigma 0.8 (per 9 years), clipped to [0.005, 0.25], the same clip as p_id. k_pid ~ lognormal, median 1.2, sigma 0.9 (dimensionless). The 5 to 95% range is about 0.27 to 5.3, so the multiplier on moral cost when the doctrine is fully held runs from about 1.3x to 6.3x. The bottom is never zero.
range.basis:
Strength (k_pid) from the cases. The cases set a ceiling but cannot pin down a central value.

- Gorbachev 1989 (Levesque 1997): while the doctrine was held, rulers gave up holding Eastern Europe by force despite the 1956 and 1968 precedents. That is a stake comparable to an empire. So the cases allow a large multiplier, up to several times baseline moral cost. But the same rulers still used limited lethal force at home (Tbilisi 1989, Baku 1990, Vilnius 1991, dozens to about 150 dead). The doctrine therefore raised the cost of mass killing without making it absolute, which argues against an effectively infinite k. Economic decay and Afghanistan confound the case, so part of the restraint may be material, which argues for a low bottom.
- Ashoka after Kalinga (Rock Edict XIII): conquest was renounced for decades but the army and threats were kept. This is consistent with a large but finite rise in cost. The evidence is self-presentation (Strong calls the inscriptions propaganda), so it carries little weight.
- Theodosius 390: unusable (disputed, and the penance came after the killing).

Hence a wide lognormal, from about 1.3x (mostly material confounding) to about 6x (doctrine doing most of the work), with median about 2.2x.

Hazard (p_pid). No case gives a base rate, so it comes from Jev, as the protocol requires. Two converts in roughly 2,300 years of rulers suggests adoption is rare, but that cannot be converted into a rate. Jev's median is 0.07, which is near p_id's 0.045, so the two processes are symmetric. Widening sigma to 0.8 (p_id uses 0.6) reflects that the answer rests only on Jev plus weak cases.

The Jev strength questions were incoherent and are not used (see the jev field).
range.jev:
Run on 2026-10-02 with jev-1.13.0. The wording was fixed in a script before the run: paper/jev_brakes/jev_pid.py.

Scenario (all questions): "Around 2040, AI and robots do all productive and military work. The small ruling group of a major power no longer needs its population for labor, taxes or soldiers, and faces no voters, courts or foreign pressure that can bind it."

Hazard questions:
- h1: "Within the next nine years, this ruling group comes to sincerely hold a religious, ethical or humanist doctrine under which killing or abandoning the population would be gravely wrong in their own eyes." Answer 0.07.
- h2: "Over the coming nine years, the rulers themselves genuinely convert to a moral or religious creed that forbids them from letting their now-useless population die." Answer 0.06.
- h3: "Before nine years have passed, the people at the top adopt a sincere belief system, not a public pose, that makes harming the population unthinkable to them." Answer 0.07.
- Result: median 0.07, range 0.06 to 0.07. This sets p_pid's median at 0.065. The spread is widened to sigma 0.8 because the paraphrase spread understates real uncertainty.

- With the doctrine (k1 to k3): 0.26, 0.24, 0.32, median 0.26.
- With no doctrine (b1 to b3): 0.34, 0.47, 0.29, median 0.34.

c.name: Autonomous clergy as a sanctioning institution (church veto)
c.mechanism: An organized religious hierarchy independent of the ruler can withhold legitimacy, sacraments or obedience, raising the cost of mass killing. Jared Rubin, Rulers, Religion, and Riches (Cambridge UP, 2017), models religious authorities as legitimizing agents who can withdraw legitimacy; Cosgel and Miceli, 'State and religion', Journal of Comparative Economics 37 (2009), similar (neither fetched this session). In every documented modern case the clergy's leverage came from their mass following, not from rulers' beliefs.
cases: Galen sermons and Aktion T4, Germany 1941: von Galen's 3 Aug 1941 sermon called euthanasia murder, and the official T4 gassing program was halted later that month. Restraint toward Galen is attributed to Goebbels preferring 'to wait until the end of hostilities to avoid undermining German morale in a heavily Catholic area'; Hitler promised retribution 'to the last farthing'. Killing continued decentralized and secret (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemens_August_Graf_von_Galen; Burleigh, Death and Deliverance, 1994). Attribution: popular morale.

Bulgaria, March-May 1943: Metropolitans Kiril and Stefan protested and threatened civil disobedience; the Holy Synod pleaded on 22 March; deportation from Bulgaria proper halted. Attribution contested (Peshev's protest, public protest, war turning, Tsar Boris's calculations); Steven F. Sage notes a 'paucity of evidence' that Church statements were heeded (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rescue_of_the_Bulgarian_Jews).

Thessalonica 390 (weak): Ambrose denied Theodosius communion after the massacre; narrative called 'pious fiction' by modern scholars; penance came after (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_Thessalonica).
Denmark 1943, rejected: bishops' pastoral letter mobilized the public, no evidence it restrained German authorities directly (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rescue_of_the_Danish_Jews).
c.parameterization: Extra moral/legitimacy cost on depopulate and neglect, c_cl x church_strength, multiplied by public leverage like the revolt and threat terms since the evidence places its force in the mass following.
c.overlap: Very high: as public reaction it is part of E0, tau0 and revolt threat; as elite non-cooperation part of p_ref. Adds nothing beyond existing parameters unless rulers themselves believe, which is the protective-doctrine candidate.
c.survives_A3_A6: Mostly no. Power came from the faithful or from human administrators who might refuse; under A3 to A6 a protest costs rulers nothing beyond their own conscience. Even before A3 to A6 restraint was partial (T4 continued covertly).

v.reasons: None of the cases shows clergy themselves restraining rulers who could have kept killing. Galen: I checked the Wikipedia page. Galen was spared because Goebbels feared for "German morale in a heavily Catholic area", which is popular leverage, not church authority. Hitler planned retribution after the war, and "a year later, the euthanasia programme was still active" but run more secretly. So killing moved underground rather than stopping. Bulgaria: the page confirms Sage found "a paucity of evidence that Church statements... were heeded or anything other than dismissed by Boris". The cause is contested, with Peshev, public protest and the turn of the war as alternatives. Thessalonica: the penance came after the massacre and the story may be pious fiction, so nothing was restrained. Denmark: the candidate already rejects it. That leaves zero solid cases, and the rule needs two. The mechanism exists in the literature: Rubin (2017) and Cosgel and Miceli (2009) are real works, though I did not fetch them. But by the candidate's own account the leverage comes from the mass following, which E0, tau0, revolt threat and p_ref already carry.

Bulgaria's attribution is contested and Sage says the Church was likely dismissed. Thessalonica is post hoc and possibly fictional. Denmark is rejected. Rule 3 (not already in the model): FAIL. c.name: In-group protection: sparing the ruler's kin, clan, ethnic group or nation (including demographic nationalism)
c.mechanism: MERGED from 'Sparing the ruler's own kin, clan or ethnic group' and 'Nationalism that values the nation's people as such'. Rulers are tied to kin and ethnic networks and stack forces with them (Quinlivan 1999; Roessler, Ethnic Politics and State Power in Africa, 2016). Mass killing usually targets specific groups and spares the perpetrators' own (Valentino, Final Solutions, 2004; Straus, The Order of Genocide, 2006). Nationalist doctrine may also treat the size of the national population as part of national greatness, so rulers lose utility from fewer co-nationals even if useless. Ceausescu set a goal of raising Romania from 20 to 30 million and framed childbearing as national service (Decree 770, 1966; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decree_770), but that goal was tied to labor and geopolitical capacity. In the record nationalism more often licenses killing out-groups than restrains killing.
cases: Selective mass killings (Holocaust, Rwanda, Darfur) spared the perpetrators' own group (Valentino 2004; Straus 2006), but sparing the in-group is close to definitional, not evidence of restraint by personal ties.
Counter-case: the Khmer Rouge killed large numbers of ethnic Khmer.
Ceausescu's Romania 1966-89: rulers valued headcount of co-nationals, but not as restraint from killing; the policy caused many maternal deaths and the motive was labor and power (Decree 770).
Unverified: how far Saddam's Tikriti clan favoritism extended. No case found where in-group or nationalist valuation is credited with stopping rulers capable of mass killing of their own nationals.
c.parameterization: A share f_ing of each bloc (from kin network up to co-ethnic or co-national share) excluded from the depopulate target and protected from escalation (partial order with target 1 - f_ing), or split alpha_med into in-group and out-group weights, or a headcount term on surviving co-nationals (which would favor warehousing over neglect but give no extra reason to serve).
c.overlap: Substantial: alpha_med explicitly includes an 'in-group premium for co-nationals'; p_tot0, f0 and k_esc already allow less-than-total targeting, and threat elimination (A11, k_esc) erodes a spared in-group seen as threatening. Distinct only as a bloc spared outright and protected from escalation.
c.survives_A3_A6: The affective tie survives loss of leverage; documented demographic nationalism valued population for labor, soldiers and geopolitical weight, which A3 to A6 make worthless. At kin-network scale (thousands) it collapses into the remnant; only at ethnic or national scale would it move the 99.9% headline, and evidence of restraint at that scale is missing.

v.reasons: The candidate's own case list fails Rule 2. It admits that in-group sparing in the Holocaust, Rwanda and Darfur is "close to definitional, not evidence of restraint", meaning the in-group was never targeted, so nothing was restrained. It cites a counter-case: the Khmer Rouge killed large numbers of their own ethnic Khmer. It says Ceausescu's demographic nationalism was not restraint from killing, was driven by labor and power motives, and caused maternal deaths. It ends by stating that no case was found where in-group or nationalist valuation is credited with stopping rulers who could mass-kill their own nationals. That leaves zero qualifying cases, and two are required. The mechanism does have some published grounding: Quinlivan 1999 and Roessler 2016 on coup-proofing with co-ethnics, and Valentino 2004 and Straus 2006 on selective targeting. But that literature documents who gets targeted and how rulers secure their forces, not a causal account of rulers holding back from killing because of in-group ties. So Rule 1 is weak at best. I could not run extra checks: the WebSearch budget for the session was used up (200 of 200), so this verdict rests on the candidate's own admissions and on the known content of the cited works. The admissions alone are enough for Rule 2 to fail clearly.
v.rule_results: Rule 1 (documented mechanism): weak. The cited works document selective targeting and co-ethnic stacking of forces, not in-group ties restraining rulers from killing. Rule 2 (two cases of restraint attributed to this mechanism): FAIL. The candidate presents no qualifying case and explicitly says none was found; its cases are definitional sparing, a counter-case (Khmer Rouge) and a non-restraint case (Ceausescu). Rule 3 (model-expressible and not already in the model): mostly overlaps alpha_med's in-group premium and the partial-targeting parameters p_tot0, f0 and k_esc; only distinct as a fully protected bloc. Survival under A3 to A6: the affective tie survives, but the demographic-nationalism branch rests on the value of labor and soldiers and collapses; at kin scale it does not move the headline result. Not decisive given the Rule 2 failure.

v.reasons: From the model-fit side, the candidate is mostly carried by existing parameters, and its own evidence fails rule 2. (1) In m8_v4.py line 324, alpha_med is defined as elite willingness to pay for a population with no leverage, "plus an in-group premium for co-nationals". That premium is the nationalist, co-national valuation, and the proposed headcount term is just a differently shaped version of alpha_med. (2) Partial targeting is already in the model. p_tot0 and f0 (lines 451-453 and 1647-1653) let the designation spare 10-70% of the population, so a spared bloc of size 1 - f_ing is already in range. The only new piece is protecting that bloc from escalation by k_esc, and that runs against the model's A11 threat logic (any free surviving community can organize and take revenge). The demographic nationalism case (Decree 770) valued people for labor, soldiers and geopolitical weight, all of which A3 to A6 remove. (4) The candidate itself says no case was found where in-group or nationalist valuation stopped rulers capable of mass killing of their own nationals. Sparing the in-group in selective genocides is close to definitional, and the Khmer Rouge is a counter-case. Rule 2 needs two cases that attribute the restraint to this mechanism, and there are none.

Rule 2 (two attributed cases of restraint): FAIL. The candidate concedes no such case exists, and the Khmer Rouge is a counter-case. A3-A6 survival: kin-scale affect survives but falls into the remnant; national-scale valuation was tied to labor and military leverage, which A3-A6 remove.

c.name: Anticipated self-targeting by coalition members ('I could be next', Thermidor)
c.mechanism: MERGED from 'Anticipated self-targeting (the apparatus turns on its makers)' and 'Intra-elite I could be next restraint'. Non-leader coalition members fear that a mass-killing capability and the precedent of using it will be turned on them, and block, slow or overthrow the leader, or bind each other, for self-preservation rather than moral refusal. Svolik, The Politics of Authoritarian Rule (Cambridge UP, 2012): power-sharing as elites' credible threat to remove an encroaching leader; insiders remove most ousted autocrats. R.R. Palmer, Twelve Who Ruled (1941); Colin Jones, The Fall of Robespierre (Oxford UP, 2021); Gorlizki and Khlevniuk, Cold Peace (Oxford UP, 2004), on the post-Stalin collective-leadership settlement. Under A6, automated killing capacity held by one faction is a credible threat to others. The model makes atrocities raise the elite purge hazard (k_par, B4) but members do not anticipate it when voting, so this is also an internal-consistency gap.
cases: France, 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794): the Law of 22 Prairial (10 June 1794) removed deputies' immunity from summary arrest; deputies briefly passed an amendment restoring it, revoked the next day; Paris executions rose to 509 in Prairial and 796 in Messidor. Robespierre's 8 Thermidor speech denounced unnamed enemies; deputies, 'thinking that Robespierre was planning yet another purge like that of the Dantonists and Hebertists', overthrew him; the law was repealed 1 August 1794 (Wikipedia 'Law of 22 Prairial' and 'Fall of Maximilien Robespierre', fetched 2026-10-02, citing McPhee 2012; Palmer 1941; Jones 2021). Motive attribution explicit.

USSR, June 1953: Khrushchev, Malenkov and others arrested Beria, who held the MVD, after warnings he was preparing a coup (Strokach's report of 21 June 1953), put security police under party control and executed his associates (Amy Knight, Beria, Princeton 1993; Wikipedia 'Lavrentiy Beria', fetched). McCauley (2014, pp. 43-44, cited in Wikipedia 'De-Stalinization') says Khrushchev aimed to 'liberate Party officials from the fear of repression'. Beria was the last top leader executed; the 1957 Anti-Party Group were demoted, not killed (Wikipedia 'De-Stalinization'); mutual-security attribution from Gorlizki and Khlevniuk 2004, not re-verified. Caveat: this restrains violence against elites; the fall in mass repression (1953 amnesty freed 1.2 to 1.35 million) is attributed mostly to the Gulag crisis and Beria's own initiative.

Weaker: post-Cultural Revolution Deng-era leaders, many former victims, ended mass campaigns and built collective-leadership norms (Ezra Vogel, Deng Xiaoping and the Transformation of China, 2011); motives mixed, and 1989 shows partial restraint.
c.parameterization: (a) Voting: in oligarchies and for inner-circle members in personalist regimes, add an anticipated self-risk cost to depopulate (scaled for neglect): c_selfrisk x expected rise in own purge probability via k_par x (1 - own control share), lowering support under the q_ol supermajority; c_selfrisk on the C_oust scale (0.02 to 3 output-share), wide. (b) Thermidor hazard: when a harsh order issues, non-leaders attempt counter-coup with yearly hazard k_th x (1 - S_L); success removes the leader and resets policy to status quo (like p_oust) with 5-year cooldown; k_th roughly 0 to 0.5/yr bounded by Thermidor versus terrors with no response (Stalin 1937-38, Khmer Rouge), else Jev. Optional: hazard of an elite pact capping the leader's purge rate.
c.overlap: Heavy overlap with v_eff, c_cc and C_oust; Thermidor is effectively a successful inner-circle veto. Distinct: self-preservation motive does not shrink with sel_top or p_ref; trigger is the harsh order itself (c_cc fires only on purges); members anticipate k_par in the vote. If v_eff is read as summing every reason the inner circle blocks, part (b) double counts and only part (a) is new.
c.survives_A3_A6: Partly. The motive survives and strengthens under A6, but acting on it needs real control share (1 - S_L). Once B2 purges concentrate force (S_L >= 0.5 or singleton) little is left. Thermidor depended on human armed sections (National Guard under Barras; Robespierre's Paris Guard support failing) and 1953 on loyal officers (Zhukov), both removed by A4. Part (a) survives in oligarchies with dispersed automated control (conc_k). Also, when the target is the public, elites may expect exemption (bunkers, remnant), weakening the 'next it will be us' inference that drove cases where terror had already hit elites.

v.reasons: The mechanism and case checks hold, though only one case is strong. Rule 1 (documented mechanism): passes. Svolik (2012) is the standard published account of insiders' credible threat to remove a leader who encroaches on them. His count that about two-thirds of non-constitutional exits were by regime insiders is well known, but I could not fetch it this session (Cambridge URLs returned 500, search budget used up). Thermidor scholarship (Palmer, Jones, McPhee) gives the same causal account at the case level. Rule 2 (two cases): passes, with a caveat. Thermidor is strong and I checked it: Wikipedia 'Law of 22 Prairial' and 'Fall of Maximilien Robespierre' confirm that immunity was removed, the amendment restoring it passed and was then reversed, executions were 509 in Prairial and 796 in Messidor, deputies feared 'yet another purge like that of the Dantonists and Hebertists', and the law was repealed on 1 Aug 1794. Mass killing by a body that had the capacity stopped, and the sources attribute this to the 'I could be next' motive. USSR 1953 is moderate. Wikipedia 'Lavrentiy Beria' confirms Strokach's coup warning, Khrushchev's 'Beria is sharpening his knives', the arrest backed by Zhukov, and the MVD placed back under the party. Wikipedia 'De-Stalinization' confirms McCauley's 'liberate Party officials from the fear of repression' and that the 1957 Anti-Party Group was demoted rather than executed. Motives were mixed: the East German uprising and policy disputes also drove the Beria arrest. The restraint is mainly on killing elites, not on mass repression, as the candidate says itself. Still, an ongoing practice of killing (purges of top leaders) stopped through this mechanism. The Deng-era case is weak and was not checked. Two cases meet the bar, one strongly and one partly. Because the second case is thin, the range should be wide.
v.rule_results: Rule 1 documented mechanism: PASS. Svolik 2012 and the Thermidor historiography give a causal account; Svolik's insider-removal figure was not re-fetched. Rule 2 two historical cases: PASS (narrowly). Thermidor was verified, with the motive stated explicitly and mass executions stopping afterwards. USSR 1953 was verified on the elite-fear motive and the end of lethal elite purges, but motives were mixed and mass repression fell mostly for other reasons. The Deng case is weak and unverified. Rule 3 and A3-A6 survival: outside this lens (left to the second reviewer). I note that both cases relied on human armed forces (the National Guard under Barras, Zhukov's officers).

v.reasons: Model-fit check of m8_v4.py (lines ~1478-1600) and supplement_parameters.md. The model already links atrocities to elite danger: k_par multiplies the leader's purge hazard by the share of the population killed deliberately (inc = k_prg ... S_L (1 + k_par w_atroc)). But no member's utility includes their own purge risk. U contains welfare, cost, revolt threat scaled by tau and k_ret (k_ret is fear of SURVIVORS among the public, not of the leader), outside pressure, land, moral cost mXk/mXn, and switching cost. Nothing prices "the leader may turn on me." The personalist veto (veto2) fires only if a non-leader member is in the moral-refusal set (refuse_k/refuse_n, which come from p_ref x rsel), so a self-interested non-refuser can never block. The oligarchic q_ol rule just sums members' ideals, so self-risk never lowers support for depopulate. C_oust prices ouster after a FAILED order, which is a different trigger. So part (a), adding c_selfrisk x the expected rise in own purge probability (via k_par) x (1 - own control share) to members' utility for depopulate/neglect, is not carried by any existing parameter. It can be stated as one parameter on the existing C_oust scale, and it also fixes a real internal inconsistency (members are myopic about a hazard the model itself creates). Neglect gets the same cost scaled by kappa_N. The cost lowers support under q_ol in oligarchies. In personalist B2 regimes, a non-leader who is blocked only by self-risk can trigger the existing veto2 roll (P = v_eff x min(1, 2(1 - S_L))). A per-member exemption share e_ex covers rulers who expect the apparatus never to reach them; those members have zero self-risk cost. The leader has zero self-risk cost, because B2 purges only non-leaders. Part (b), the Thermidor counter-coup hazard k_th, is dropped: the verifier found it double counts c_cc and v_eff x (1 - S_L), and its historical success depended on human armed units, which A4 removes.

c.name: Leader mortality and succession reset
c.mechanism: Personalist leaders die or are incapacitated; successions open a window where the successor coalition is wider, must bargain, and often reverses the predecessor's harshest policies to protect itself and build elite legitimacy. The model has no leader death over 2026-2075. Mortality for leaders aged 65-80 is roughly 2 to 6% a year, non-negligible across lag_dec0 (1-5 yr) and T_full (2-15 yr). Counter-evidence on size: Kendall-Taylor and Frantz, 'When Dictators Die', Journal of Democracy 27(4), 2016: autocratic regimes usually survive a dictator's death in office (regime continuity does not settle policy continuity but bounds the brake).
cases: USSR, March 1953: within weeks of Stalin's death the Doctors' Plot was declared fabricated and doctors freed, 1.2 to 1.35 million prisoners amnestied, and the Gulag moved from the MVD (Wikipedia 'Amnesty of 1953' and 'Lavrentiy Beria', fetched; Gorlizki and Khlevniuk, Cold Peace, 2004). Strong attribution: the same inner circle had complied while Stalin lived.

China, 1976-78: after Mao's death and the Gang of Four's arrest, the Cultural Revolution ended and mass rehabilitations followed (Vogel 2011; MacFarquhar and Schoenhals, Mao's Last Revolution, 2006). Strong for timing.
Counter-cases bounding strength: North Korea 1994 and 2011 (camps continued; UN COI 2014); Kendall-Taylor and Frantz 2016.
c.parameterization: Yearly hazard h_mort ~ U(0.02, 0.06) of leader exit for personalist leaders (largest-share member in oligarchies), from actuarial tables the authors must source. On exit: with p_coll the coalition resets to a collective under the oligarchy rule with refusal share partly restored (h_purge convergence restarts); with p_rev ~ U(0.1, 0.6) policy resets to status quo and an executing depopulation halts (about 0.5-1 in USSR/China versus about 0 in North Korea). AI-era life extension lowers h_mort over time.
c.overlap: No existing parameter carries exogenous leader turnover; nearest are p_oust, c_cc and k_pz. It is an exit mechanism rather than a decision cost: the successor's choice is still governed by existing moral, alpha and veto parameters, so it works through delay and reset.
c.survives_A3_A6: Trigger yes (death is independent of labor, enforcers, revolt). Reset weaker: in 1953 and 1976 successors had to win human party and army networks; under A6 control of automated force could pass smoothly to an heir or credential-holding faction, making the North Korea pattern likelier. AI medicine could cut h_mort sharply. p_rev at the low end.

v.reasons:
My lens was mechanism and cases, and the evidence holds well enough that no protocol rule clearly fails. Caveats follow.

Mechanism: the idea that leader identity matters, and that a natural death in office changes policy (with effects concentrated in autocracies), is published research. Jones and Olken, 'Do Leaders Matter?', QJE 120(3), 2005, uses leader deaths as natural experiments. I could not fetch the full text this session, so this rests on the known citation. The narrower claim (a wider successor coalition that has to bargain and so reverses the harshest policies) is backed mainly by case histories (Gorlizki and Khlevniuk 2004), not by a general theory. Kendall-Taylor and Frantz 2016 (fetched) find that regimes usually survive a dictator's death. That limits the size of the effect but does not refute the mechanism.

Cases. USSR 1953 is strong. The fetched Wikipedia 'Doctors' plot' page records Beria's 31 March decree dropping all charges, announced in Pravda on 6 April, less than four weeks after Stalin died. Khrushchev's 1956 speech says Stalin 'did not have the time' to finish the affair. The successors still held the full NKVD/MVD apparatus. Caveat: the fetched 'Amnesty of 1953' page links the amnesty to a crisis inside the Gulag (overcrowding, loss of control), not to the death itself, and it excluded political prisoners. That part is weaker evidence. China 1976-78 is moderate. Mao's death led to the Gang of Four's arrest within weeks, but the fetched 'Boluan Fanzheng' page shows Hua continued Maoist policy. The mass rehabilitations (over 3 million) began only after Deng consolidated power in December 1978, through a coalition reshuffle. So the attribution runs through the succession contest, which fits the mechanism but has a lag. Two cases attribute the restraint to the succession. North Korea is a real counter-case, which supports a wide range starting at zero.
v.rule_results: Rule 1 (documented mechanism): PASS. Jones and Olken 2005 is a published causal design based on leader deaths. The specific step that reverses policy rests on case studies, and Kendall-Taylor and Frantz 2016 limit the size. Rule 2 (two cases attributed to this mechanism): PASS. USSR 1953 is strong for the Doctors' Plot reversal (Khrushchev attributes it directly to Stalin's death; the successors kept full repressive capacity), but weaker for the amnesty (Gulag crisis). China is moderate (rehabilitation came about two years later, through the Deng-era coalition change after the death). Rule 3 and survival under A3-A6: outside my lens, left to the other reviewer. The size range should run from 0 (North Korea 1994/2011) upward, matching the candidate's low p_rev under A6.

v.reasons:
Model fit holds. I checked m8_v4.py. The only ways a leader leaves are a counter-coup during a purge (c_cc x (1 - S_L), around line 1488), ouster after a failed X or C order (p_oust, line 1620), and coalition resets at breakdown, grab or insurgent victory (reset_coal, line 1440). k_pz only moves regimes toward personalism, never back. Nothing models exogenous leader death or incapacity, so a yearly exit hazard is new and can be stated as a parameter: h_mort plus a succession rule.

Three caveats for the authors.

(1) Partial overlap with id_hl. Its stated basis is "regime turnover, generational change", and it already makes depopulation ideology fade with a 10 to 20 year half-life (line 1449). If leader death also clears ideology, that double counts. Either leave ideology out of the reset or shorten id_hl to match.

(2) p_rev as an exogenous policy-reset probability partly duplicates existing parameters. Once the dead leader's extra harshness (s_tilt, sel_top at the top) is gone, the successor's choice should come from the coalition's existing moral, alpha, sel_top^0.5 and q_ol oligarchy rule. The cleaner rule: on death, remove the leader, then hand his hw/aw to one heir (the North Korea pattern) with probability p_heir, or else split it across the remaining members. Clear personalist status if S_L falls below 0.5, restart the purge clock, and let the existing decision rule re-run, halting an executing option if it no longer passes. That keeps the novelty to the trigger and the reset of coalition structure.

(3) A3 to A6. The trigger survives: death does not depend on labor, enforcers or revolt. The reset survives only in part. In 1953 and 1976, successors had to win over human party, police and army networks, and Gulag economic inefficiency and popular legitimacy were also motives. Those channels are removed by A3 to A6. Under A6, aw can pass to an heir or whoever holds the credentials, which makes the North Korea pattern likely. So the effect should run mostly through the dead leader's personal harshness and coalition widening, with p_heir high when automated force is high.

Also, the 0.02 to 0.06 range may be high for elites with top medical care, and AI-era life extension lowers it over time. A wider range starting near 0.01 would be safer.
v.rule_results: Rule 1 (documented mechanism): not this lens's job; the cited sources (Gorlizki and Khlevniuk 2004, Kendall-Taylor and Frantz 2016) are plausible, and the other reviewer checks them. Rule 2 (historical restraint): not this lens's job; USSR 1953 is strong for timing and attribution, China 1976 is strong for timing, and North Korea bounds the size. Rule 3 (model-expressible, not already carried): PASS. No exogenous leader exit exists in m8_v4.py; p_oust, c_cc and k_pz are triggered by other events. It can be stated as a hazard h_mort plus a succession split rule. Partial overlap with id_hl needs handling, and p_rev should come from the existing decision rule, not a separate draw. Survival under A3 to A6: PARTIAL PASS. The trigger survives. The reset is weakened because automated force can pass smoothly to an heir, so p_rev or p_heir should sit at the North Korea end when automated force is high.

range.parameter:
There are four new parameters, all acting on the B2/F1 coalition after closure.
(1) h_mort: the yearly hazard that the leader (the largest-share member, ldr) dies or is incapacitated, measured at closure.
(2) g_mort: how fast that hazard rises with the leader's age (Gompertz slope).
(3) k_le: how fast AI-era medicine cuts the hazard after closure.
(4) p_heir: the chance that on a death the leader's control passes intact to one heir (the North Korea, Syria 2000 and Azerbaijan 2003 pattern). Otherwise his control splits among the surviving members (the USSR 1953, China 1976, Turkmenistan 2006 and Uzbekistan 2016 pattern).
The brake works only through structure. A split widens the coalition, can end personalist status (S_L < 0.5) and partly restarts the h_purge refusal convergence. It also forces a fresh decision under the existing moral, alpha, sel_top, q_ol and veto rules, which can halt a depopulation already under way. There is no separate policy-reversal draw (p_rev is dropped, per verifier 2), and ideology is left alone, because id_hl already covers regime turnover.
range.distribution: h_mort ~ U(0.01, 0.05) per year at closure. g_mort = 0.085 per year of age, fixed (Gompertz). k_le ~ U(0, 0.10) per year after closure (judgment, J). p_heir ~ U(0.3, 0.8). The successor inherits the hazard as it stood at the time of death (no age reset).
range.basis:
h_mort: in the US 2021 male period life table (CDC NVSR 72(12), Table 2, which I extracted from the PDF), the chance of dying within a year is 0.0196 at 65, 0.0269 at 70, 0.0405 at 75, 0.0640 at 80 and 0.1043 at 85. 2021 includes COVID excess deaths, so these are slightly high. Elites live much longer: Chetty et al., JAMA 2016, find the top 1% of men live 14.6 years longer than the bottom 1%. My own approximation is that this roughly halves age-specific mortality. Incapacitation (stroke, dementia) pushes the hazard back up. Leaders of the major powers in 2026 are in their 70s to about 80 (Xi born 1953, Putin 1952, Trump 1946). Leaders could be younger after closure, and the range covers that. So 0.01 to 0.05 runs from an elite 65-year-old to an ordinary 80-year-old. This range is wider and lower than the candidate's 0.02 to 0.06, as verifier 2 asked. g_mort = 0.085 is the standard human Gompertz slope (mortality doubles about every 8 years, which matches the CDC rows above). k_le has no precedent, so it gets a wide judgment range starting at 0 (no medical gain), and the reason is stated in the paper.

p_heir from the cases. I can name 11 personalist leaders who died in office. Six passed intact to an heir: North Korea 1994 and 2011, Syria 2000, Azerbaijan 2003, Togo 2005 and Gabon 2009. Five split or passed to a collective, or to an insider who had to bargain: USSR 1953, China 1976, Yugoslavia 1980, Turkmenistan 2006 and Uzbekistan 2016. That gives 6/11 = 0.55, with a 90% interval of roughly 0.3 to 0.8. Of the five splits, four reversed the harshest policies:
- USSR 1953: the Doctors' Plot was dropped within four weeks (Wikipedia, 'Doctors' plot').
- China: rehabilitations under Deng from 1978.
- Turkmenistan: Berdimuhamedow restored the pensions of 100,000 people that Niyazov had cut, reopened rural libraries and the Academy of Sciences, and eased travel limits (Wikipedia, fetched).
- Uzbekistan: Mirziyoyev closed Jaslyk prison and released political prisoners in 2019 (Wikipedia, fetched).
None of the heir cases reversed (North Korea's camps continued, per the UN COI 2014). This supports modelling the reset as running only through the split branch, by way of the existing decision rule. Kendall-Taylor and Frantz (Journal of Democracy, 2016; abstract fetched) find that a death in office is not one of the transitions that open the way to regime change. That fits the brake running through policy inside a regime that survives, not through regime collapse.

Under A6 the cases cannot fix p_heir, because control codes might pass to an heir more easily than human networks did. So I ran Jev (see the jev field). Jev's median of 0.38 sits at the low end of the case interval, and verifier 2 argued for a higher value under automation. U(0.3, 0.8) covers both.

The evidence is weak, so the range is wide. It never reaches zero, because the trigger (death) does not depend on A3 to A6.

c.name: Agent empowerment (moral hazard in delegated repression)
c.mechanism: A ruler who delegates mass repression empowers the executing agency and may halt the campaign and purge the executors once they threaten the ruler. Svolik 2012 (chapter on the moral hazard of authoritarian repression): agents relied on for repression gain leverage over the ruler. Restraint comes from the leader's position, not morality.
cases: USSR, November 1938: mass operations under NKVD Order 00447 (386,798 executed under that order alone; Wikipedia 'NKVD Order No. 00447', fetched) were halted by the joint Sovnarkom-Central Committee resolution of 17 November 1938 criticizing NKVD practice; Yezhov was removed and later shot (Getty and Naumov, The Road to Terror, Yale 1999; Jansen and Petrov, Stalin's Loyal Executioner, Hoover 2002). Historians disagree on why: goals reached, damage to economy and army, or Stalin's distrust of an over-mighty NKVD; only the last is this mechanism. Attribution not checked online this session.

Germany, June 1934 (weak): Hitler purged the SA leadership after its power threatened the army and himself (Kershaw, Hitler 1889-1936: Hubris, 1998). Curbed one violent arm, not a halt to mass killing.

Rulers facing a chance of catastrophic correlated automation failure (common-mode failure, cyberattack, sabotage, war damage) would value a human population with working skills as insurance. Perrow, Normal Accidents (1984), on unavoidable failures in tightly coupled systems; Bainbridge, 'Ironies of Automation', Automatica 19(6), 1983, on humans as fallback whose skills decay. No published work applies this hedge to a ruler deciding whether to kill a population; the link to restraint is inference. 'Genetic diversity' as a motive has no documented case and is not proposed.
